crane-lift-quick.formula: Gross load = load + rigging + block + jib_deduct. Per-leg sling tension L = W / (n × sin(theta)) with the sling angle theta measured from horizontal (vertical pick theta = 90 deg gives W/n; tension diverges as the sling flattens). Percent of chart = gross / chart_capacity × 100. Flags: < 75% green, 75-90% yellow, ≥ 90% red. Refuses to render an output without the user-entered chart capacity (the tool never reproduces a load chart).
crane-lift-quick.edition: ASME B30.5 (Mobile and Locomotive Cranes) by name and section. ASME B30.9 (Slings) for the per-leg formula. OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC (cranes and derricks) by section.
crane-lift-quick.freeAccess: ASME B30 series licensed; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 free at ecfr.gov.
crane-lift-quick.governance: Estimate. Engineer of record governs the design and acceptance. Verify against the project structural drawings and the manufacturer's published capacity / chart.
crane-lift-quick.editionNote: Single-edition (ASME B30.5 / B30.9 + OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC). The crane manufacturer's load chart and the qualified lift director govern.

assumptions.name: Per-leg formula
assumptions.value: L = W / (n × sin(theta)) with theta the sling angle from horizontal; vertical pick (theta = 90 deg) L = W / n

assumptions.name: Critical-lift threshold
assumptions.value: 75% of chart capacity (engineering-practice critical-lift trigger)

septic-tank-for-interval.formula: Tank working volume = target_years x occupants x accumulation_per_person_per_year / fill_fraction (the inverse of years = tank x fill / (people x accumulation)).
septic-tank-for-interval.edition: USEPA Onsite Wastewater Treatment Systems Manual (EPA/625/R-00/008); university onsite-wastewater extension pumping-frequency guidance, by name.
septic-tank-for-interval.freeAccess: Free at epa.gov/septic. Extension pumping-frequency tables free on land-grant university extension sites.
septic-tank-for-interval.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
septic-tank-for-interval.editionNote: The inverse of septic-pumpout-interval: the tank working volume that puts a target number of years between pumpings. A planning estimate -- the state minimum tank size by bedroom count usually governs the actual tank, and a sludge-judge measurement, not a calendar, governs the pumping call.

assumptions.name: Default accumulation
assumptions.value: 30 gal per person per year of net sludge + scum (a garbage disposal roughly doubles it); editable

assumptions.name: Default fill fraction
assumptions.value: 0.33 of the tank before pumping; editable

assumptions.name: Code minimum governs
assumptions.value: state minimum tank sizes by bedroom count usually govern the actual tank, overriding this interval-based estimate

pipe-partial-flow-depth.formula: A = (D^2/8)(theta - sin theta); P = D theta/2; R = A/P; y = (D/2)(1 - cos(theta/2)); solve (1.486/n) A R^(2/3) sqrt(S) = Q for theta by bisection on the rising branch (0, 5.27811]; V = Q/A; tau = 62.4 R S. Max discharge at theta = 5.27811 (d/D = 0.9382), max velocity at tan theta = theta, theta = 4.49341 (d/D = 0.8128).
pipe-partial-flow-depth.edition: Manning's equation applied to circular-segment geometry for partial (part-full) gravity flow, the standard sewer-design relation as compiled in ASCE/WEF MOP FD-5 (Gravity Sanitary Sewer Design and Construction) and Chow's Open-Channel Hydraulics, by name; the 2 ft/s self-cleansing velocity is standard sewer practice.
pipe-partial-flow-depth.freeAccess: Manning's equation and the circular-segment geometry are public results; the partial-flow relations here are derived from them rather than read from a proprietary chart.
pipe-partial-flow-depth.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pipe-partial-flow-depth.editionNote: The partial-flow normal depth of a circular gravity pipe: Manning Q = (1.486/n) A R^(2/3) sqrt(S) applied to the circular segment A = (D^2/8)(theta - sin theta), P = D theta/2, y = (D/2)(1 - cos(theta/2)), solved for the central angle theta by bisection. Discharge is NOT monotonic with depth - it reaches a maximum about 7.6% above the full-bore value at d/D = 0.938 and falls back to the full value at the crown, while velocity peaks at d/D = 0.813. Both turning points are DERIVED from the geometry (5 A' P = 2 A P' for discharge, A' P = A P' i.e. tan theta = theta for velocity), not taken from a tabulated chart. Because two depths satisfy most flows, the solver is restricted to the rising branch and returns the SMALLER root, which is the physical normal depth. The hydraulic radius is D/4 at both half-full and full, so a half-full pipe runs the same velocity as a full one on the same slope. Reports the 2 ft/s self-cleansing check and the boundary (tractive) shear tau = 62.4 R S. Assumes steady uniform flow and a roughness n held CONSTANT with depth; Camp's variable-n curves raise n at shallow depths, so a low d/D result is slightly optimistic. It does not cover surcharged or pressurized flow, gradually varied (backwater) profiles, or non-circular conduits. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record's design or the local sewer code.

assumptions.name: Circular-segment geometry
assumptions.value: A = (D^2/8)(theta - sin theta), P = D theta/2, y = (D/2)(1 - cos(theta/2))

assumptions.name: Non-monotonic discharge
assumptions.value: Q peaks ~7.6% above full-bore at d/D = 0.938; the smaller (physical) root is reported

assumptions.name: Self-cleansing
assumptions.value: 2 ft/s minimum velocity; boundary shear tau = 62.4 R S reported alongside

assumptions.name: Constant roughness
assumptions.value: n held constant with depth; Camp's variable-n curves are not applied

ujoint-operating-angle.formula: single Cardan joint: output speed ranges cos(b) to 1/cos(b) of input, twice per rev; peak-to-peak variation = 1/cos(b) - cos(b) = sin^2(b)/cos(b). Two-joint cancellation requires equal working angles (within ~1 deg) and in-plane yoke phasing.
ujoint-operating-angle.edition: Cardan (Hooke) universal-joint kinematics and the two-joint cancellation rule, by name; the U-joint / driveshaft manufacturer's angle-vs-rpm chart (Spicer / Dana, GMB) and the vehicle service manual govern.
ujoint-operating-angle.freeAccess: The Cardan velocity relation is public kinematics; the working angles come from the measured driveline geometry, and the maximum-angle-vs-rpm limit is on the manufacturer's chart.
ujoint-operating-angle.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ujoint-operating-angle.editionNote: A single Cardan (Hooke) universal joint does not transmit rotation uniformly when the two shafts meet at an operating angle b: as the joint turns, the driven-shaft speed oscillates between cos(b) and 1/cos(b) times the driving speed, completing two full cycles per revolution. The peak-to-peak speed non-uniformity is therefore 1/cos(b) - cos(b), which equals sin^2(b)/cos(b) -- about 3.1% at a 10 degree angle, only 0.3% at 3 degrees, but 6.9% at 15 degrees; and because it is the fluctuating ANGULAR ACCELERATION (which grows with rpm squared) that actually excites driveline vibration, small angles matter more at higher speed. A conventional two-joint driveshaft is designed to CANCEL this: the second joint introduces an equal and opposite fluctuation, but only when two conditions both hold -- the two joints' working angles are equal (practically, within about a degree) AND the shaft's two yokes are phased in the same plane (in-phase, the usual slip-yoke arrangement). If the angles are unequal or the yokes are clocked wrong, the fluctuations do not cancel and a second-order (2/rev) vibration results. The practical setup targets are thus a small working angle at each joint -- a common rule of thumb keeps each under roughly 3 degrees at highway rpm, with the allowable angle falling as rpm rises -- and equal angles at the two ends. This tile reports the per-joint speed variation and the equal-angle cancellation check; the exact maximum permissible working angle for a given driveshaft rpm comes from the U-joint and driveshaft manufacturer's published chart (Spicer / Dana, GMB, American Axle), and the vehicle service manual and the actual measured transmission-output, driveshaft, and pinion inclinations govern the alignment.

assumptions.name: Cardan velocity variation
assumptions.value: output speed cos(b) to 1/cos(b) of input, 2/rev; peak-to-peak = 1/cos(b) - cos(b) = sin^2(b)/cos(b)

assumptions.name: Two-joint cancellation
assumptions.value: cancels only with equal working angles (within ~1 deg) and in-plane yoke phasing; keep each angle small (rule of thumb < ~3 deg at highway rpm)

pump-eff-w2w.formula: Water HP WHP = (GPM × TDH) / 3960. Brake HP estimate BHP = motor_kW × 1.341 × motor_eff × drive_eff. Wire-to-water % = WHP / motor_HP × 100. Categories: ≥ 65% good, ≥ 50% ok, < 50% degraded.
pump-eff-w2w.edition: Hydraulic Institute (HI) standards by name; ANSI/HI 14.6 (Rotodynamic Pumps for Hydraulic Performance Acceptance Tests) by name.
pump-eff-w2w.freeAccess: HI standards licensed; principles free in published pump-engineering texts.
pump-eff-w2w.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.

assumptions.name: Constant 3960
assumptions.value: (550 ft-lb/sec/HP × 60 sec/min) / (8.34 lb/gal × 1 ft height) ≈ 3960

sling-angle.formula: Per-leg tension L = W / (n × cos(θ/2)) for basket / bridle slings at included (apex) angle θ (tension is W/n with legs vertical and diverges as the legs open toward horizontal); vertical L = W / n; choker reduction factor 0.75 applied per ASME B30.9.
sling-angle.edition: ASME B30.9 (Slings) by name and section.
sling-angle.freeAccess: ASME B30.9 licensed; principles free at OSHA 29 CFR 1910.184 (free at ecfr.gov) and at major manufacturer (Crosby, Lift-It) technical pages.
sling-angle.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.

assumptions.name: Choker derate
assumptions.value: 0.75 (ASME B30.9 typical)

supply-pressure-budget.formula: elevation_loss = fixture_height * 0.433; available = street_pressure - elevation_loss - meter_loss - bfp_loss - friction_loss; headroom = available - fixture_min; adequate = headroom >= 0. 0.433 psi per foot of water column.
supply-pressure-budget.edition: IPC 2021 Section 604 and the ASPE Plumbing Engineering Design Handbook Vol. 2 by name; first-principles pressure budget.
supply-pressure-budget.freeAccess: IPC 2021 free read-only at codes.iccsafe.org; the 0.433 psi/ft water-column constant is public.
supply-pressure-budget.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
supply-pressure-budget.editionNote: Use the minimum recorded street pressure. IPC 2021 Table 604.3 minimum flow pressures: 8 psi for lavatories, sinks, showers, laundry trays and hose bibbs; 20 psi for a tank or flushometer-tank water closet and for thermostatic or pressure-balance shower and tub valves; 25 psi for a urinal flush valve; 35 psi for a siphonic and 45 psi for a blowout flushometer-valve water closet. IPC 604 caps static pressure at 80 psi (a PRV is required above it and adds its own loss).

assumptions.name: Water column
assumptions.value: 0.433 psi per foot of elevation

assumptions.name: Fixture minimum default
assumptions.value: 8 psi (lavatory, sink, shower); tank water closet 20, urinal valve 25, siphonic flushometer valve 35, blowout flushometer valve 45 psi

polymeric-sand-bags.edition: Polymeric joint-sand bag-count identity by name (area over the per-bag coverage, plus waste); first-principles arithmetic.
polymeric-sand-bags.freeAccess: The bag-count arithmetic is public first-principles; the coverage per bag comes from the product chart.
polymeric-sand-bags.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
polymeric-sand-bags.editionNote: The coverage per bag comes from the product chart and drops sharply with wider and deeper joints (and rises with larger pavers, which have fewer joints per square foot). Polymeric sand is swept in, compacted, and activated with a light water mist. Distinct from the paver and base takeoff in paver-patio.

assumptions.name: Coverage per bag
assumptions.value: ~75 sf/bag for tight joints, dropping to roughly 22-42 sf/bag for wide joints (Techniseal SmartSand, Alliance Gator Maxx G2 charts); the product chart governs

assumptions.name: Waste
assumptions.value: ~5% default for the sweep-in and activation

ppv-fan-sizing.formula: effective_cfm = fan_cfm x entrainment_efficiency; air_change_min = volume_cf / effective_cfm; clearing_min = air_change_min x ln(1 / remaining_fraction); required_cfm = volume_cf x ln(1/f) / (efficiency x target_time_min).
ppv-fan-sizing.edition: Positive-pressure ventilation clearing time as a well-mixed dilution problem -- the contaminant falls exponentially, so clearing to a remaining fraction f takes ln(1/f) air changes -- with the fan's rated free-air flow reduced by an entrainment efficiency, by name. Public physics. The incident commander, department SOPs, and a gas meter reading govern when a structure is clear.
ppv-fan-sizing.freeAccess: The dilution relation is public physics. The structure volume, fan rating, entrainment efficiency, and target are the crew's own values.
ppv-fan-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ppv-fan-sizing.editionNote: A positive-pressure fan's rated flow is measured in free air at the fan face, and what actually reaches the structure is less: the cone has to seal the doorway, some air spills, and the exhaust opening has to be sized to let the air out. An entrainment efficiency somewhere in the range of half to seven tenths is the working assumption, and the effective flow is what the arithmetic should use. The clearing time is a dilution problem rather than a displacement one, and that distinction is the whole point. Air entering a room mixes with what is already there instead of pushing it out as a plug, so the contaminant falls exponentially: each air change removes about sixty-three percent of what remains, reaching ninety percent clear takes 2.3 air changes and ninety-nine percent takes 4.6. A crew that gives the fan one air change and goes in finds the building still charged. The shape of that curve also means the last increment is the expensive one, since going from ninety to ninety-nine percent clear costs as long again as everything before it. And because the effective flow is set by the exhaust opening as much as by the fan, halving the opening doubles the time with the same fan, which makes the opening the more important decision.

assumptions.name: Dilution, not displacement
assumptions.value: well-mixed exponential decay; ln(1/f) air changes to reach a remaining fraction f

assumptions.name: Entrainment efficiency
assumptions.value: roughly 0.5 to 0.7 of the fan's free-air rating actually reaches the structure

assumptions.name: The opening governs
assumptions.value: the exhaust opening sets the effective flow; halving it doubles the clearing time with the same fan

tailstock-setover.formula: S = OAL x (D - d) / (2 L); per-inch setover = (D - d) / (2 L). When L = OAL it reduces to S = (D - d) / 2.
tailstock-setover.edition: Lathe tailstock setover for taper turning between centers - first-principles as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
tailstock-setover.freeAccess: Pure geometry, public; the offset comes from the part length and the taper diameters.
tailstock-setover.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tailstock-setover.editionNote: First-principles setup geometry. The tailstock setover S = OAL x (D - d) / (2 L) offsets the tailstock center so a part turned between centers cuts a taper. The offset scales with the OVERALL length between centers, not the taper length, because the whole workpiece pivots about the headstock center; when the taper runs the full length it reduces to (D - d)/2. The tailstock is offset toward the tool (toward the operator on a front-tool-post lathe) to put the small diameter at the tailstock end. The method suits shallow tapers only - it swings the center holes off the true axis, so the produced angle is slightly off and center-hole/contact wear grows with the offset; a taper attachment or the compound slide governs steep or precise tapers. A machine-setup aid; check the first part.

assumptions.name: Overall length
assumptions.value: OAL is the full length between centers; the setover scales with it, not the taper length

assumptions.name: Shallow tapers
assumptions.value: the method swings the centers off axis, so it suits shallow tapers; steep tapers need a taper attachment or compound

cylinder-storage-separation.formula: separation is satisfied when the distance between oxygen and fuel-gas cylinders or combustible materials is at least 20 ft, OR when a barrier is present that is simultaneously noncombustible, at least 5 ft high, and rated at least one-half hour. Handling adds two independent conditions: cylinders secured upright, and valve protection caps in place and secured.
cylinder-storage-separation.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.350, a US federal regulation in the public domain, quoted directly.
cylinder-storage-separation.freeAccess: 29 CFR is published in full at no cost by OSHA and the eCFR.
cylinder-storage-separation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cylinder-storage-separation.editionNote: The provision everyone half-remembers as a 20 foot rule is an OR, and the alternative is usually the cheaper compliance path: a noncombustible barrier at least 5 ft high with a fire-resistance rating of at least one-half hour. On a tight site, 20 ft of clear floor is expensive and a 5 ft barrier is not, so knowing the alternative exists is worth more than knowing the distance. But the barrier route carries THREE conditions that must all hold, and two of them fail silently. A sheet of plywood is the right shape and stands the right height, and it satisfies neither the noncombustible condition nor the rating - and nobody measures a fire-resistance rating on a jobsite, so the failure is invisible at a glance. The tile names which of the three failed rather than reporting a bare no. The scope of the separation is also wider than it usually gets applied: it runs to fuel-gas cylinders OR COMBUSTIBLE MATERIALS, especially oil or grease. Oxygen stored 20 ft from the acetylene and hard against the parts washer, the oil drums, or a rag bin has not addressed the hazard the rule exists for, because oxygen enrichment makes ordinary combustibles behave in ways nobody is expecting. Two handling requirements travel with the storage question and are checked alongside it: cylinders secured in an upright position at all times except for short periods while actually being hoisted or carried, and valve protection caps in place and secured - the cap being what stands between a knocked-over cylinder and a sheared valve. Not checked: whether cylinders are in use rather than in storage, which changes what applies; acetylene-specific storage and the waiting period after a cylinder has been on its side; regulator, hose, and torch condition; flashback arrestors and check valves; prohibited hoisting by caps, magnets, or slings; transport in enclosed vehicles; indoor storage and its quantity limits; and NFPA 55 or state rules, which are often stricter. A screen, not a gas-storage plan; 1926.350, the gas supplier, and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Distance route
assumptions.value: a minimum of 20 ft between oxygen and fuel gas or combustibles

assumptions.name: Barrier route
assumptions.value: noncombustible AND at least 5 ft high AND at least a half-hour rating

assumptions.name: Either satisfies
assumptions.value: the provision is an OR, not a distance requirement with an exception

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: combustible MATERIALS, especially oil or grease, not only fuel-gas cylinders

assumptions.name: Upright
assumptions.value: secured upright except briefly while being hoisted or carried

assumptions.name: Caps
assumptions.value: valve protection caps in place and secured

weld-passes-arc-time.formula: passes = ceil(A_groove / a_pass); weight = A_groove x length x density; arc_h = weight / dep_rate; total_h = arc_h / op_factor.
weld-passes-arc-time.edition: The standard welding-cost estimating relations (passes, deposited weight, arc time, operator factor), by name.
weld-passes-arc-time.freeAccess: The deposited-weight and arc-time estimating relations are standard welding-cost references (AWS / Lincoln / Miller estimating guides). The WPS and the shop's measured rates govern.
weld-passes-arc-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
weld-passes-arc-time.editionNote: Weld-metal volume drives welding cost: passes = ceil(groove area / area per pass); deposited weight = groove area x length x density (steel ~0.283 lb/in^3); arc-on time = weight / deposition rate; and with an operator (duty) factor, total shop time = arc time / factor. Doubling the groove doubles the passes and the arc time. This returns the count and time estimate: it assumes uniform passes of the entered area, is arc-on time (the operator factor, often 20-40% for manual work, captures the fit-up/repositioning/slag time between arcs), and is not a full cost model. A planning estimate; the WPS and the shop's measured rates govern.

assumptions.name: Volume-driven
assumptions.value: passes = ceil(area/a_pass); weight = area x length x density (steel ~0.283 lb/in^3)

assumptions.name: Arc-on time
assumptions.value: arc_h = weight / deposition rate; total = arc / operator factor

assumptions.name: Uniform passes
assumptions.value: assumes uniform passes of the entered area; not a full cost model

tank-volume-dished-heads.formula: shell = [R^2 acos((R-h)/R) - (R-h) sqrt(2Rh-h^2)] L; heads = (b/R)(pi h^2/3)(3R-h), b = R/2 (2:1 elliptical) or R (hemispherical); full = pi R^2 L + (b/R)(4/3) pi R^3.
tank-volume-dished-heads.edition: Horizontal-tank partial gauging - the straight shell is the circular-segment prism and the two dished heads form an ellipsoid whose partial fill is an affine-scaled spherical cap; standard tank-gauging geometry as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press) and API 2551 manual-tank-strapping practice, by name; public domain.
tank-volume-dished-heads.freeAccess: Public-domain solid geometry; the diameter, shell length, depth, and head type are user-supplied.
tank-volume-dished-heads.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tank-volume-dished-heads.editionNote: Partial volume of a horizontal cylindrical tank with dished (curved) heads from a dipstick depth - the head-type correction the flat-end tank-volume tile leaves out. The straight shell is the circular-segment prism, area = R^2 acos((R-h)/R) - (R-h) sqrt(2Rh-h^2) times the seam-to-seam shell length; the two curved heads together form an ellipsoid of revolution, so their partial fill is the spherical cap scaled by the head depth, V_heads = (b/R)(pi h^2/3)(3R-h), with b = R/2 for a 2:1 semi-elliptical (ASME dished) head and b = R for a hemispherical head. Enter the straight-shell length, not the overall length - the heads are added on. A torispherical (ASME flanged-and-dished) head holds only about two-thirds of a 2:1 elliptical head (Brighton Tru-Edge: 323 vs 501 gal at 96 in), so the elliptical option overstates an F&D tank; the tank's strapping chart governs custody transfer. Reported in cubic feet and US gallons with the percent full.

assumptions.name: Shell partial volume
assumptions.value: circular-segment prism, area x shell length (the flat-end tank-volume result)

assumptions.name: Head partial volume
assumptions.value: (b/R)(pi h^2/3)(3R-h), b = R/2 elliptical or R hemispherical

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: 2:1 elliptical or hemispherical heads; flat heads are the tank-volume tile; torispherical (F&D) is overstated, since an F&D head holds about two-thirds of a 2:1 head

overrun-percent.formula: overrun% = (mix_weight - finished_weight) / finished_weight x 100 for equal volumes; air% = (mix_weight - finished_weight) / mix_weight x 100.
overrun-percent.edition: Goff & Hartel, Ice Cream, 7th ed.; FDA 21 CFR 135.110 standard of identity, by name.
overrun-percent.freeAccess: 21 CFR 135.110 is public/free at ecfr.gov; the food-science overrun definition is standard.
overrun-percent.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
overrun-percent.editionNote: Overrun is the air whipped into frozen dessert, measured by weighing equal volumes of mix and finished product. Federal standard: finished ice cream must weigh at least 4.5 lb/gal and carry at least 1.6 lb of total solids per gallon. Bands: gelato/premium ~20-35%, standard ~50-90%, economy/soft-serve ~90-100%. Freezer type, fat, solids, and draw temperature all move the number; the weighed cup is the shop measurement of record.

assumptions.name: FDA minimum density
assumptions.value: finished ice cream >= 4.5 lb/gal and >= 1.6 lb total solids/gal

assembly-r-value.formula: U_assembly = framing factor x 1/R_framing-path + (1 - factor) x 1/R_cavity-path; R = 1/U; framing path adds stud depth x 1.25 R/in.
assembly-r-value.edition: ASHRAE Handbook of Fundamentals parallel-path (isothermal-planes) method (by name).
assembly-r-value.freeAccess: ASHRAE Fundamentals licensed; air-film and material R-values widely published free.
assembly-r-value.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
assembly-r-value.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice / first-principles take-off; refresh as practice and product data shift).

assumptions.name: Framing factor
assumptions.value: ~0.25 at 16 in o.c., 0.22 at 24 in o.c.; softwood ~1.25 R/in (editable)

defrost-cycle-sizing.formula: sensible_btu = frost_lb x 0.5 x (32 - coil_temp_f); latent_btu = frost_lb x 144; coil_warmup_btu = coil_mass x specific_heat x rise; meltwater_btu = frost_lb x 1.0 x (drain_temp_f - 32); total_btu = (sensible + latent + melt water warmed to the drain temperature + coil warm-up) / defrost_efficiency; defrost_min = total_btu / heater_btuh x 60.
defrost-cycle-sizing.edition: Defrost heat from the sensible, latent, and coil warm-up terms -- 144 BTU/lb to melt ice, about 0.5 BTU/lb-F to warm it to 32 F -- divided by the defrost efficiency, by name; public thermodynamics with the efficiency entered rather than bundled. The equipment manufacturer's defrost data and a measured coil temperature at termination govern.
defrost-cycle-sizing.freeAccess: The latent heat of fusion and the specific heat of ice are public physical constants; the frost load, coil mass, heater rating, and efficiency are the system's own values.
defrost-cycle-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
defrost-cycle-sizing.editionNote: Three terms make up a defrost and they are not the same size. Melting the ice costs a hundred and forty-four BTU per pound against roughly twenty to warm that same ice from a freezer coil's temperature up to thirty-two degrees, so the latent term dominates -- but the coil warm-up term is the one that gets forgotten, and on a large coil with heavy fin stock it is real. Defrost efficiency captures everything that is not melting frost: heat going into the box instead of the coil, into the drain pan, and out through the insulation, and on electric defrost it is commonly only sixty to eighty percent, which means a fifth to two fifths of the heater's output is a direct load on the refrigeration system. The last relation closes the loop and is the useful part. Frost accumulates at the coil's moisture removal rate, which is set by the box's latent load from door openings, product respiration, and infiltration, and that determines how much frost is on the coil when defrost initiates, which determines how long defrost takes. A box with heavy traffic therefore needs more defrosts and each one is longer, and every minute of defrost is a minute of heat going into a freezer. A controller's fixed termination time is right for exactly one frost load, which is the whole argument for demand defrost.

assumptions.name: Latent dominates
assumptions.value: 144 BTU/lb to melt against about 0.5 BTU/lb-F to warm the ice to 32 F

assumptions.name: Defrost efficiency
assumptions.value: entered because it varies widely by coil, case and termination (the 80% default is optimistic for electric display-case defrost per ORNL); the rest is heat into the box

assumptions.name: Frost load drives time
assumptions.value: a fixed termination time is correct for exactly one frost load -- the argument for demand defrost

blast-fume-clearance-time.formula: concentration decays as exp(-Q t / V); one air change = volume / airflow; the air changes to a target fraction = ln(100 / target percent); clearance time = the two multiplied; the airflow for a target time = volume x changes / that time.
blast-fume-clearance-time.edition: The perfect-mixing dilution relation by name, with atmospheric testing by calibrated instrument named as the actual re-entry requirement rather than an alternative to it. The mine ventilation plan, the blaster in charge, and MSHA govern.
blast-fume-clearance-time.freeAccess: Exponential-decay arithmetic on the user's own heading and airflow figures; no regulatory re-entry criterion is reproduced.
blast-fume-clearance-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
blast-fume-clearance-time.editionNote: Perfect-mixing dilution decays exponentially, so each air change removes the same FRACTION rather than the same amount. One change takes a heading to 37% of the starting concentration, two to 14%, three to 5%, and 4.6 to 1%. That is the shape that makes intuition fail: the first minute does most of the work and the last decade of concentration takes as long as everything before it, so a crew re-entering early on the belief that most of it clears fast is walking into a real fraction of the original fume load. Two field cautions belong with the number. Real headings do not mix perfectly -- dead corners, the muck pile, and a tubing end set too far back all leave pockets that clear far more slowly than the average, which is why the required practice is to TEST the atmosphere with a calibrated instrument before re-entry rather than to trust a clock. And fumes continue to be released from the muck pile and from any misfire long after the shot, so a heading that tests clean at the portal can still be unsafe at the face. The calculation sets the minimum wait; the gas detector sets the actual one. The airflow lever is worth seeing: raising delivered flow cuts clearance proportionally, and on a heading turning several rounds a day that is real time.

assumptions.name: Each change removes a FRACTION
assumptions.value: 37% remains after one, 14% after two, 1% after 4.6

assumptions.name: Real headings mix imperfectly
assumptions.value: dead corners and the muck pile hold fumes far longer than the average

assumptions.name: The instrument sets the wait, not the clock
assumptions.value: and continued fume generation is not modelled at all

ras-svi-settleability.formula: Xr = 1,000,000 / SVI; ras_ratio = MLSS / (Xr - MLSS); Q_RAS = ras_ratio x Q.
ras-svi-settleability.edition: Settleability-based RAS from the sludge volume index (WEF MOP / Sacramento activated-sludge manuals), by name.
ras-svi-settleability.freeAccess: The settleability-based RAS relation is public wastewater-operations material; the settleability and clarifier performance govern the actual return.
ras-svi-settleability.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ras-svi-settleability.editionNote: The achievable return concentration Xr = 1,000,000 / SVI is the settleability ceiling, not a guaranteed value - clarifier depth, loading, and temperature move it. Poor settling (a high SVI) forces a higher return rate, and a bulking sludge can make a target MLSS unreachable within the pump capacity. This is the settleometer path to the same mass balance ras-flow-rate does from a measured RAS_SS. The settleability and clarifier performance govern - an operating aid, not a process design.

assumptions.name: Settleability ceiling
assumptions.value: the achievable return concentration is about Xr = 1,000,000 / SVI mg/L

assumptions.name: Higher SVI, higher RAS
assumptions.value: poor settling forces a higher return ratio; a bulking sludge can make a target MLSS unreachable within pump capacity

pv-energy-yield.formula: annual_kwh = dc_kw x psh x 365 x perf_ratio; specific_yield = annual_kwh / dc_kw; capacity_factor = annual_kwh / (dc_kw x 8760); monthly_kwh_avg = annual_kwh / 12.
pv-energy-yield.edition: NREL PVWatts energy model (E_annual = P_dc x PSH x 365 x PR) and the standard specific-yield and capacity-factor definitions, by name; the relations are public.
pv-energy-yield.freeAccess: The PVWatts energy model and the specific-yield and capacity-factor definitions are public NREL relations; PVWatts is free at pvwatts.nrel.gov.
pv-energy-yield.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pv-energy-yield.editionNote: The NREL PVWatts energy model E_annual = P_dc x PSH x 365 x PR, with specific yield = E / P_dc and capacity factor = E / (P_dc x 8760). The peak-sun-hours is the plane-of-array daily irradiation from NREL's NSRDB / PVWatts for the site, tilt, and azimuth (not a fixed 5); the performance ratio (default 0.77, a typical whole-system ratio including temperature loss; it equals the retired PVWatts V1 derate -- current PVWatts uses 14% losses and a 96% inverter, 0.826) varies with climate, soiling, and equipment and is the single biggest lever on the estimate; the first-year figure degrades roughly half a percent a year. A pre-design estimate, not a bankable production model.

assumptions.name: Annual energy
assumptions.value: annual kWh = DC nameplate x peak-sun-hours x 365 x performance ratio (PVWatts)

assumptions.name: Performance ratio
assumptions.value: PR (default 0.77) rolls up soiling, shading, mismatch, wiring, inverter, and availability losses

assumptions.name: Benchmarks
assumptions.value: specific yield = annual / DC (kWh per kW); capacity factor = annual / (DC x 8760)

rain-on-snow-surcharge.formula: applies = (0 < pg <= pm,max) AND (slope_deg < W/50), pm,max = 25 / 30 / 35 / 40 psf for risk category I / II / III / IV; total = pf + (applies ? 8 psf : 0).
rain-on-snow-surcharge.edition: The ASCE 7-22 §7.10 rain-on-snow surcharge load, by name.
rain-on-snow-surcharge.freeAccess: ASCE 7 is available through the ASCE Library at ascelibrary.org; the §7.10 trigger and surcharge are public.
rain-on-snow-surcharge.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rain-on-snow-surcharge.editionNote: ASCE 7-22 §7.10 adds a rain-on-snow surcharge to the balanced flat-roof snow load Pf where the ground snow load Pg is no more than pm,max (Table 7.3-4: 25, 30, 35, or 40 psf for risk category I, II, III, or IV) AND the roof slope in degrees is less than W/50, with W the horizontal eave-to-ridge distance in feet. ASCE 7-22 sets the surcharge at 8 psf; 7-16 added 5 psf where Pg was 20 psf or less. The change recognizes that a low-slope roof in a warm wet-snow climate retains rain that a steeper roof would shed. The surcharge applies only to the balanced load case and only where both triggers are met; it is not added to a steep roof or a high-ground-snow (Pg > pm,max) region, and it does not apply to drift, sliding, or partial-load cases. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Trigger
assumptions.value: 0 < Pg <= pm,max (25 / 30 / 35 / 40 psf by risk category) and slope (deg) < W/50

assumptions.name: Surcharge
assumptions.value: 8 psf added to the balanced Pf only

assumptions.name: Balanced only
assumptions.value: not added to drift, sliding, or partial-load cases

max-rpm-from-piston-speed.formula: rpm_max = 6 x mps_limit_fpm / stroke_in (the mean-piston-speed relation MPS = stroke x RPM / 6 solved for RPM); mps_limit_ms = mps_limit_fpm x 0.00508.
max-rpm-from-piston-speed.edition: The mean-piston-speed relation MPS = 2 x stroke x RPM solved for the RPM cap, the inverse of the mean-piston-speed tile, as compiled in the engine-building references, by name.
max-rpm-from-piston-speed.freeAccess: The mean-piston-speed relation is a public engine-building result; the regime bands are standard builder guidance.
max-rpm-from-piston-speed.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
max-rpm-from-piston-speed.editionNote: The maximum safe engine speed for a chosen mean-piston-speed ceiling, the inverse of the mean-piston-speed tile: from MPS = stroke_in x RPM / 6 (ft/min), the RPM cap is 6 x MPS_limit / stroke. Mean piston speed sets the inertial load on the rods, pins, and bearings independent of bore, so a chosen ceiling gives a safe redline for the stroke, and a longer stroke lowers the cap for the same limit. The practical ceilings are ~4,000 ft/min street/endurance, 4,000-4,500 performance, over 4,500 race (exotic parts). This uses the average (not peak) piston speed; the bands are guidance for typical materials, and a specific assembly's limit depends on the rods, pistons, and pins. A shop aid; the component makers' rpm ratings govern.

assumptions.name: RPM cap
assumptions.value: rpm_max = 6 x mps_limit_fpm / stroke_in

assumptions.name: Regime bands
assumptions.value: street/endurance ~4,000, performance 4,000-4,500, race over 4,500 ft/min

assumptions.name: Average not peak
assumptions.value: uses the average piston speed; a specific assembly's limit depends on the rods, pistons, and pins

pitot-traverse-average.formula: V_i = 4005 sqrt(VP_i) at each equal-area point; V_avg = mean(V_i); A = (w x h)/144; CFM = V_avg x A. The single-average-VP shortcut V = 4005 sqrt(mean VP) reads high because sqrt is concave.
pitot-traverse-average.edition: Pitot-traverse airflow averaged per ASHRAE Fundamentals / AABC / NEBB field practice: average the point velocities, not the velocity pressures. By name.
pitot-traverse-average.freeAccess: The V = 4005 sqrt(VP) standard-air relation and the average-the-velocities traverse method are standard published air-balancing procedures.
pitot-traverse-average.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pitot-traverse-average.editionNote: The methodologically-correct Pitot-traverse average: convert each equal-area point's velocity pressure to a velocity V = 4005 sqrt(VP) for standard air (0.075 lb/ft^3, sea level), average the VELOCITIES, then CFM = average velocity x duct cross-sectional area. Averaging the velocity pressures first and taking one square root reads high, because the square root is concave (Jensen's inequality) -- the tile reports that over-read against the average velocity so a technician can see the size of the shortcut error. Space the points on an equal-area or log-Tchebycheff traverse and use enough of them; enter the air density at altitude or high temperature (air-density-correction gives it), where the result is otherwise a standard-air equivalent. A field measurement, not a substitute for a calibrated flow station or the equipment's own airflow rating.

assumptions.name: Air density
assumptions.value: optional (added 2026-10-09): V = 4005 sqrt(VP x 0.075/rho), the standard-air constant scaled for the entered density (the exact form is 1096.2 sqrt(VP/rho)); 0.075 lb/ft^3 leaves it unchanged

assumptions.name: Velocity from VP
assumptions.value: V = 4005 sqrt(VP) for standard air, per point

assumptions.name: Correct average
assumptions.value: average the point velocities, not the velocity pressures

assumptions.name: Standard air
assumptions.value: 0.075 lb/ft^3 unless an air density is entered; air-density-correction gives the density at altitude or high temperature

flow-continuity.formula: V2 = V1 (D1/D2)^2 (from Q = A V constant, A = pi/4 D^2).
flow-continuity.edition: The continuity equation for an incompressible fluid, by name.
flow-continuity.freeAccess: The continuity equation Q = A V is a standard fluid-mechanics relation. The code velocity limits and the engineer of record govern.
flow-continuity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flow-continuity.editionNote: Continuity: for an incompressible fluid the volumetric flow Q = A V is constant, so the velocity changes with the inverse square of the diameter, V2 = V1 (D1/D2)^2. Reducing the pipe accelerates the flow (a 4-to-2 in reduction quadruples the velocity, often past the erosion limit); expanding it slows the flow and converts the velocity head back to pressure (a diffuser). This returns the downstream velocity for the entered sizes: it assumes full, incompressible flow (a gas or two-phase flow does not obey this) and does not compute the pressure change or the fitting loss at the transition. A design aid; the code velocity limits govern.

assumptions.name: Continuity
assumptions.value: V2 = V1 (D1/D2)^2 from Q = A V constant

assumptions.name: Incompressible full flow
assumptions.value: full pipe, incompressible; a gas/two-phase flow does not obey this

assumptions.name: No transition loss
assumptions.value: does not compute the pressure change or the fitting loss at the size change

concrete-depth-for-cracking-moment.formula: fr = 7.5 x lambda x sqrt(f'c); h = sqrt( 6 x Mcr / (fr x b) ), the inverse of Mcr = fr b h^2/6; S = b h^2/6; Mcr_lbin = Mcr_kipft x 12000.
concrete-depth-for-cracking-moment.edition: The ACI 318-19 cracking moment Mcr = fr Ig/yt (19.2.3.1 modulus of rupture), solved for the section depth, by name.
concrete-depth-for-cracking-moment.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; the cracking-moment and 19.2.3 rupture provisions are in the published code.
concrete-depth-for-cracking-moment.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
concrete-depth-for-cracking-moment.editionNote: The total section depth that reaches a target ACI 318-19 cracking moment for a given width, the inverse of Mcr = fr b h^2/6: h = sqrt( 6 Mcr / (fr b) ), with the modulus of rupture fr = 7.5 x lambda x sqrt(f'c) psi (19.2.3.1; lambda 1.0 normalweight, 0.75 all-lightweight). A common use is to enter 1.2 Mcr for the minimum-flexural-reinforcement check (the design flexural strength must reach at least 1.2 Mcr). It uses the gross rectangular section with the reinforcement transform neglected (the standard approximation); a T-beam or heavily reinforced section uses the transformed gross moment of inertia, and the flexural, shear, and deflection design still govern the final depth. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Section depth
assumptions.value: h = sqrt( 6 Mcr / (fr b) ), the inverse of Mcr = fr b h^2/6

assumptions.name: Rupture stress
assumptions.value: fr = 7.5 x lambda x sqrt(f'c) psi (lambda 1.0 NW, 0.75 LW)

assumptions.name: Gross section
assumptions.value: reinforcement transform neglected; the flexure/shear/deflection design still governs the depth

pipe-insulation-for-condensation.formula: Tdp from the ambient RH (saturation-vapor-pressure psychrometrics); minimum wall from the outer-surface balance h (2 pi r2/12)(Tamb - Tdp) = 2 pi (k/12) (Tdp - Tpipe)/ln(r2/r1), with k per inch, solved for r2; thickness = r2 - r1.
pipe-insulation-for-condensation.edition: Standard cylindrical-conduction and surface-film heat balance (the same public engineering relations as the landed insulation-thickness and pipe-heat-loss-radial tiles) with the dew point from the catalog's pinned psychrometric functions; no standard table reproduced.
pipe-insulation-for-condensation.freeAccess: The conduction/film balance and Magnus-form psychrometrics are public engineering relations; manufacturer condensation-control design guides publish the equivalent tables free.
pipe-insulation-for-condensation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pipe-insulation-for-condensation.editionNote: The MINIMUM wall that holds the jacket exactly at the dew point - industry practice rounds UP to the next stock wall and designs to the WORST sustained (design-day) RH, not the average. Assumes still air (1.65 BTU/hr-ft^2-F outside film, the same public reference value the hot-pipe sibling uses) and an intact vapor retarder: a torn jacket moves the condensation inside the insulation, which no thickness fixes. Near-saturation inputs error out rather than extrapolate (at 100% RH no finite wall keeps a cold surface dry). Energy sizing is the separate insulation-thickness tile. Manufacturer condensation tables and the mechanical code govern.

assumptions.name: Dew point source
assumptions.value: computed from the repo's pinned saturation-vapor-pressure / dew-point functions, not a lookup

assumptions.name: Film coefficient
assumptions.value: 1.65 BTU/hr-ft^2-F still-air default, identical to the insulation-thickness sibling; or computed (added 2026-10-09) from Churchill-Chu natural convection and gray-body radiation at the jacket emissivity, OD and dew-point surface

assumptions.name: Vapor retarder
assumptions.value: assumed continuous; failure moves condensation inside the insulation

advance-warning-sign-spacing.formula: Table 6C-1 A/B/C spacings by road type: urban low 100/100/100, urban high 350/350/350, rural 500/500/500, expressway 1,000/1,500/2,640 ft; sign positions upstream of the transition = A, A+B, A+B+C.
advance-warning-sign-spacing.edition: MUTCD Table 6C-1, Suggested Advance Warning Sign Spacing, from the FHWA Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices - a US-government public-domain work, extracted from the FHWA PDF rather than a secondary summary.
advance-warning-sign-spacing.freeAccess: The MUTCD is published free at mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov and is in the public domain.
advance-warning-sign-spacing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
advance-warning-sign-spacing.editionNote: The letters read BACKWARD from the way a crew sets signs: A is the distance from the transition or point of restriction to the sign CLOSEST to the work, B is between the first and second signs, C is between the second and third, and the standard states that the third sign is the first one a driver encounters. Reporting A/B/C alone invites someone to place the first sign 500 ft out and stop, so this tile reports cumulative distances measured upstream from the transition - the last number is where the advance warning area begins. MUTCD 6C.04 adds that on rural highways the first warning sign should sit 8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph, and that the advance warning area should extend 1,500 ft or more for open highway conditions; both are checked. These are SUGGESTED distances and the urban speed category is determined by the highway agency per the table's own footnote; site distance, sight lines, and intersections routinely force adjustment. The taper is the separate traffic-taper-length tile; buffer space, channelizing-device spacing, and flagger stations are not modeled. The MUTCD as adopted by your state and the agency's traffic control plan govern.

assumptions.name: Public-domain table
assumptions.value: MUTCD Table 6C-1 reproduced verbatim; it is a US-government work, not a copyrighted table

assumptions.name: A/B/C direction
assumptions.value: A is transition-to-nearest-sign; the third sign is the first a driver sees

assumptions.name: Rural placement guidance
assumptions.value: first warning sign 8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph; area 1,500 ft or more on open highway

egc-parallel-raceways.formula: Each parallel raceway carries a full-size EGC sized from Table 250.122 to the WHOLE circuit's overcurrent device rating; total EGC runs = number of raceways. The EGC is not divided among the parallel sets.
egc-parallel-raceways.edition: NEC 250.122(F), equipment grounding conductors for conductors in parallel, by section number - the 2023-and-earlier rule; no table is reproduced here because the sizing is delegated to this catalog's existing egc-sizing model.
egc-parallel-raceways.freeAccess: The NEC is viewable free through the NFPA online access portal; 250.122 is in every adopted edition.
egc-parallel-raceways.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
egc-parallel-raceways.editionNote: The mistake this tile exists to catch: sizing the EGC from the divided per-raceway current instead of the whole circuit's overcurrent device. A 400 A feeder in two raceways takes two full-size EGCs sized to 400 A, not to 200 A - the ungrounded conductors divide the load, the EGC does not divide the fault. The reason is fault current: a ground fault in one raceway returns through THAT raceway's EGC alone, not through all of them sharing the job, so each must carry the full available fault current long enough for the device to open. WATCH THE EDITION: this is the 2023-and-earlier rule, and the 2026 NEC revises 250.122(F) so the EGC in each raceway need not be larger than the largest ungrounded conductor in that raceway - check which edition your jurisdiction has adopted. 250.122(B) proportional upsizing for voltage-drop-upsized conductors still applies (that is the egc-upsize-proportional tile), as does the 250.122(A) rule that an EGC never needs to exceed the circuit conductors. The NEC as adopted and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Full size per raceway
assumptions.value: each raceway's EGC is sized to the whole circuit's OCPD, not the divided current

assumptions.name: Sizing delegated
assumptions.value: the Table 250.122 lookup comes from the landed egc-sizing model, not a duplicated table

assumptions.name: Edition sensitive
assumptions.value: the 2026 NEC revision caps the EGC at the largest ungrounded conductor in the raceway

mold-cleaning-labor.formula: labor_hours = affected_sf x passes / production_sf_per_hr; crew_hours = labor_hours / crew_size.
mold-cleaning-labor.edition: Source-removal multi-pass cleaning labor method (HEPA vacuum / damp wipe / HEPA vacuum) under ANSI/IICRC S520, by name. Field-labor arithmetic, not edition-bound.
mold-cleaning-labor.freeAccess: The labor roll-up is public estimating arithmetic; the multi-pass source-removal method is named in the published ANSI/IICRC S520.
mold-cleaning-labor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
mold-cleaning-labor.editionNote: Single-edition (the labor arithmetic does not roll). The Condition, substrate, and access GOVERN the production rate, and non-cleanable porous materials are removed (not counted here), not cleaned. This is a labor screen, not a remediation protocol. ANSI/IICRC S520 names the source-removal method.

assumptions.name: Production rate
assumptions.value: 100 ft^2/hr per pass is a starting rate; the Condition, substrate, and access govern the real rate

assumptions.name: Passes
assumptions.value: a default of 2 (vac / wipe, or vac / vac) with a third pass common; the field method governs

steam-prv-napier.formula: choked = downstream_p_psia < 0.58 x upstream_p_psia; capacity W = 51.5 x discharge_coeff x orifice_area_in2 x upstream_p_psia [lb/hr] (saturated, choked).
steam-prv-napier.edition: Napier's formula / ASME/API 520 / Grashof steam orifice / PRV capacity, by name.
steam-prv-napier.freeAccess: Napier's formula is a classical, published steam-flow relation; ASME/API and the valve manufacturer govern the actual certification.
steam-prv-napier.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
steam-prv-napier.editionNote: Flow chokes when the downstream absolute pressure is below 58% of the upstream, and the capacity then depends only on the upstream pressure (dropping the downstream further does not increase it). Napier is for saturated steam (superheat needs a Ksh factor). A liquid Cv, which scales with the square root of pressure drop, is wrong for choked steam, which is linear in the upstream pressure. The discharge coefficient (about 0.6 sharp-edged orifice, near 1 nozzle) must be applied. ASME/API and the valve manufacturer govern - a sizing aid, not a relief-valve certification.

assumptions.name: Choked flow
assumptions.value: chokes at P2 < 0.58 x P1; capacity then depends only on the upstream pressure

assumptions.name: Saturated steam
assumptions.value: Napier is for saturated steam; superheat needs a Ksh factor; apply the discharge coefficient

adhesive-bond-area.formula: bond area = bond length x bond width and capacity = area x shear strength; the bond length that just carries a required load is that relation inverted, and the capacity at a service temperature is the same area times the strength at that temperature.
adhesive-bond-area.edition: A capacity calculation using a shear strength the user supplies. Published adhesive strengths are for a specific substrate, surface preparation, bond line thickness, cure schedule, and test temperature, and the achieved strength in a field joint depends on all of them; surface preparation usually governs and is not represented in this arithmetic at all. It does not address peel or cleavage loading, stress concentration at the bond ends, or the combination of bonding with welds and rivets that most modern repairs specify.
adhesive-bond-area.freeAccess: One multiplication; no adhesive strength table is reproduced.
adhesive-bond-area.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
adhesive-bond-area.editionNote: The arithmetic is trivial and everything important is in the conditions attached to the strength. Bead width is a structural dimension: an 18 in flange at 0.75 in carries 33,750 lb at 2,500 psi, and the same flange at a 0.5 in bead carries 22,500 lb -- a third of the joint gone from a dimension nobody measured (width across the load; a longer overlap along it adds little, per the Henkel LOCTITE design guide). Bond line thickness has an OPTIMUM rather than a minimum, which is why manufacturers hold it with glass beads and why clamping until the adhesive squeezes out makes the joint weaker. Structural adhesives also lose strength as they warm, so the data sheet's value at the SERVICE temperature is the number the joint has. A bonded joint outside the vehicle manufacturer's procedure is an unapproved repair with crash-performance consequences.

assumptions.name: The shear strength is entered
assumptions.value: it is conditional on substrate, preparation, bond line, cure, and temperature
assumptions.source: the adhesive manufacturer's technical data sheet

assumptions.name: Surface preparation is not modelled
assumptions.value: it is usually the governing variable and is absent from the arithmetic

assumptions.name: Shear only
assumptions.value: peel and cleavage are resisted far less well and are not computed
assumptions.source: the vehicle manufacturer's body repair manual

step-drawdown-efficiency.formula: the step-drawdown relation s = BQ + CQ^2, with B (aquifer loss) and C (well loss) fitted by least squares from the entered steps by plotting s/Q against Q; well efficiency = BQ / (BQ + CQ^2), and specific capacity = Q / s.
step-drawdown-efficiency.edition: Step-drawdown testing as AWWA A100 and standard hydrogeologic practice state it. The steps are ENTERED from a field test in which drawdown was allowed to stabilise at each rate.
step-drawdown-efficiency.freeAccess: One published relation and a two-parameter least-squares fit.
step-drawdown-efficiency.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
step-drawdown-efficiency.editionNote: The linear term is formation loss, a property of the aquifer that no work on the well improves; the quadratic term is turbulent loss at the screen and pack, and it is what degrades over a well's life and what rehabilitation recovers. EFFICIENCY DEPENDS ON THE RATE YOU TEST AT, which is the trap -- well loss goes with the SQUARE of flow, so a well that is 62% efficient at its operating rate can be 83% efficient at a third of it, and a light-duty test finds nothing wrong with a well that is in trouble where it actually runs. THE TREND IS WORTH MORE THAN THE NUMBER: a well's efficiency when new is the baseline later tests are read against, and the same well losing twenty points over five years at the same rate is incrusting.

assumptions.name: Steps must be stabilised
assumptions.value: drawdown still moving at a step biases the fit

assumptions.name: Test at the operating rate
assumptions.value: efficiency is rate-dependent because well loss is quadratic

assumptions.name: Not an aquifer test
assumptions.value: transmissivity and storativity come from a constant-rate test

scaffold-tie-spacing.formula: height-to-base ratio = height / the minimum base dimension, with outriggers substituting their effective base; the maximum free-standing height is the limit ratio times that base, so the first tie goes at or below it; tie rows and ties per row follow the entered spacings.
scaffold-tie-spacing.edition: The OSHA 1926.451(c)(1) height-to-base rule by name -- a supported scaffold whose height exceeds four times its minimum base dimension must be restrained from tipping. Tie SPACINGS are entered from the manufacturer's instructions and the applicable requirements; the tie's own capacity and its anchorage are separate and usually govern. Sheeting multiplies the lateral load and requires a re-evaluated pattern. OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L, the scaffold manufacturer's instructions, and the competent person govern.
scaffold-tie-spacing.freeAccess: One ratio and two divisions; no manufacturer tie table is reproduced.
scaffold-tie-spacing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
scaffold-tie-spacing.editionNote: The 4-to-1 ratio is a THRESHOLD rather than a design: it is the point at which a scaffold can no longer be relied on to stand on its own. The first tie therefore goes at or BELOW that height, and a scaffold erected past the ratio with its first tie higher has an unbraced length below it that is exactly the failure geometry. Outriggers work by widening the base, which is the denominator, so they raise the free-standing height directly. Sheeting changes the problem entirely -- a wrapped scaffold is a sail, and wrapping an erected scaffold without re-evaluating the ties is a recognized cause of collapses. And the tie itself has to go to something: a tie anchored to a window frame, a gutter or trim is not resisting a lateral load, and a tie pattern correct on the drawing and anchored to cladding is a scaffold with no ties at all.

assumptions.name: Tie spacings are entered
assumptions.value: they come from the manufacturer's instructions for the type and height

assumptions.name: Tie and anchor capacity are separate
assumptions.value: and are usually what governs

assumptions.name: No wind calculation
assumptions.value: the sheeted flag is a reminder, and the re-evaluated pattern comes from a qualified person

raised-floor-tile-airflow.formula: Q = 4,005 x discharge coefficient x free area in sq ft x sqrt(plenum pressure in w.c.); pressure at fixed geometry varies with flow squared.
raised-floor-tile-airflow.edition: The standard orifice airflow relation. Tile manufacturer measured flow curves and an under-floor pressure survey govern.
raised-floor-tile-airflow.freeAccess: A public orifice relation and square-law inversion.
raised-floor-tile-airflow.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
raised-floor-tile-airflow.editionNote: A raised floor distributes fan airflow; it does not create it. Opening more tiles at fixed system airflow lowers each tile's share and required pressure, while local pressure and leakage make actual distribution nonuniform.

assumptions.name: Discharge coefficient is entered
assumptions.value: a tile maker's chart is better than 0.7: Tate's DirectPerf 25% tile prints 357 CFM at 0.02 in. and 496 at 0.04, which fits about 0.62, so 0.7 reads about 13% high
assumptions.source: Tate Airflow Panels & Controls, Performance Charts

assumptions.name: Free area
assumptions.value: gross tile area times entered open-area fraction

assumptions.name: Discharge coefficient
assumptions.value: entered coefficient represents the selected tile geometry

anode-bed-resistance.formula: Dwight single anode R = 0.00521 rho / L x [ln(8L/d) - 1]; Sunde bed R_N = 0.00521 rho / (N L) x [ln(8L/d) - 1 + (2L/S) ln(0.656 N)], rho in ohm-cm and lengths in feet.
anode-bed-resistance.edition: Dwight's and Sunde's groundbed relations for uniform soil. A Wenner resistivity survey at the bed's own depth and the CP designer govern.
anode-bed-resistance.freeAccess: Public relations published in the CP literature.
anode-bed-resistance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
anode-bed-resistance.editionNote: A bed is not its anodes in parallel: they compete for the same soil. Length sits outside the logarithm and diameter inside it, so drill deeper rather than auger wider.

assumptions.name: Soil
assumptions.value: uniform resistivity assumed; a layered profile changes the answer

assumptions.name: Mutual interference
assumptions.value: the Sunde term, which the naive parallel figure omits

pallet-rack-beam-capacity.formula: Two equal point loads at the quarter points: M = P L / 4; stress on 0.88 M plus a vertical impact of 25% of one unit load at a quarter point (ANSI MH16.1 2.3, ASD combination 5), not in deflection; d = P a (3 L^2 - 4 a^2) / (24 E I) with a = L/4 and E = 29,000,000 psi; allowable bending stress = Fy / 1.67; acceptance limit L/180.
pallet-rack-beam-capacity.edition: ANSI MH16.1 Design, Testing and Utilization of Industrial Steel Storage Racks, the applicable building code, and the rack manufacturer's published beam capacity AT the installed span.
pallet-rack-beam-capacity.freeAccess: The beam relations and the L/180 criterion are public; ANSI MH16.1 itself is a purchased standard.
pallet-rack-beam-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pallet-rack-beam-capacity.editionNote: Deflection governs an ordinary rack beam because it grows as the cube of span while moment grows linearly, so a bay respaced in the field has a capacity nobody recalculated and a span-specific load plaque that is now wrong.

assumptions.name: Load pattern
assumptions.value: two equal pallets delivering point loads at the quarter points

assumptions.name: Beam end connector
assumptions.value: not evaluated; its capacity comes from testing and frequently limits the beam first
